question: DP systems and speculation: logical vs padded drafter rows, CPU allreduce, queue/prefill alignment, final-rank prefix locality with API2, exact-size Engram and packed exchange, and DeepEP communication alternatives. Current AG/RS backend is not DeepEP; Engram is host offload with embedding_across_dp, resolve sharded versus shared allocation. Existing scheduler/MBT/static prefill interval is the comparator before complex policy. k5 fixed adaptiveOFF seq64 MBT16384 means the draft reservation saving is at most256 tokens/rank (not a speedup). Decoder SWA replay is deliberately approximate and disabled: separate quality lane, not a free correctness-preserving activation. DSpark acceptance diagnostics never replace sampler correctness. Use BASS and CacheRoute as mechanism context; do not assume their algorithms are drop-in. Extract source inefficiency, proposed fix, hardware/shape applicability, strongest contrary evidence and specific uncertainty that can change selection. Our live H200 topology is TP1/DP4/EP4 per replica, two replicas, seq64; no new GPU experiment exists. Quotes must be short exact passages, not a copied benchmark table.

Purpose
When a target FULL CUDA graph pads its request count,
DPSyncState.num_reqs
describes graph capacity rather than the number of scheduled requests. Reusing that capacity for uniform drafter steps makes active DP ranks select larger draft graphs than needed.
This PR keeps the DP-wide maximum real request count alongside graph capacity and uses it for uniform drafter dispatch. It also shrinks online dummy-rank DFlash batches coherently across input preparation, graph dispatch, attention metadata, EPLB preparation, and draft generation. Startup graph capture retains its required capacity.
Test Plan & Result
The performance validation below uses the official nightly build at the PR base. This PR uses the same nightly plus only the four Python files changed by this PR; the runtime SHA-256 values were verified after the overlay was applied.

power-of-two blocks of ranks, then one concurrent exchange between blocks,

Overview
DFlash and DSpark reserve
max_num_new_slots_for_drafting
draft slots per request in the scheduler token budget (K for DFlash, K − 1 for DSpark), but neither drafts in the target batch. This PR sets those slots to 0 and instead caps running requests (
max_num_active_seqs
) at
max_num_batched_tokens // num_lookahead_tokens
, so the separate draft pass still fits its buffers.
Fixes
#52922
.
Claims
DFlash/DSpark requests no longer pay for draft slots. A DSpark decode with K = 5 is charged 6 tokens instead of 10. With
--max-num-batched-tokens 512
that raises running requests from 52 to 64 and output throughput from 1373 to 3390 tok/s (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark on GB300, table below).
The draft pass stays within its
max_num_batched_tokens
-row buffers. A request cap does this instead of the slots, and it only binds when
max_num_seqs × num_lookahead_tokens > max_num_batched_tokens
.
This applies to DFlash on both model runners and to DSpark (MRV2-only), through the shared scheduler config. Slot accounting for P-EAGLE, PARD and draft models is unchanged.
Validation
Unit tests
, this revision (rebased on
f26d9f4
), one GB300 node:
pytest tests/test_config.py tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash2.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_causality.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_lookahead.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_profile.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dspark_topk.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_mtp.py tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_warmup_blocks.py
Result: 1137 passed, 5 skipped (ROCm-only), 1 failed. The failure,
test_is_encoder_decoder[meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-False]
, needs a gated repo and fails on
main
too.
New test
test_block_drafters_cap_requests_instead_of_draft_slots
, for DFlash and anchor-sampling DSpark, checks that admission stops at
max_num_batched_tokens // num_lookahead_tokens
and that admitted prompts are scheduled in full. It fails if the cap is removed or main's draft-slot charges return, and the DSpark case fails if the cap divides by K + 1.
pre-commit passes, including mypy.
End to end
, this PR against
main
(
f26d9f4
), same build and node:
Setup: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark (K = 5), TP4 on one GB300,
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 vllm serve ... --max-num-seqs 64 --max-num-batched-tokens 512 --no-enable-prefix-caching
.
Load:
vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 256 --random-output-len 1536 --random-range-ratio 0.33 --ignore-eos --temperature 0 --max-concurrency 128 --num-prompts 512 --seed 0
, with
vllm:num_requests_running
scraped every 2 s. One run per side.
--max-num-batched-tokens 512
main
this PR
Max running requests
52
64
Output throughput (tok/s)
1373

TPOT p50 / p99 (ms)
29.2 / 63.5

TTFT p50, incl. queueing (s)

Acceptance length

Variability: the previous revision, measured the same way with 2048 prompts and two interleaved runs per side, gave 51 vs 64 running and 1354 vs 3448 tok/s, within 2% of these numbers.
With
--max-num-seqs 128
, this PR runs up to 85 requests (2167 tok/s). The request cap is 102 (512 // 5) and does not bind: each decode schedules 1 + K = 6 tokens, so the 512-token budget fills at 85.
With the default budget, greedy outputs for 20 fixed prompts are byte-identical between
main
and this PR (3197 completion tokens).
Measured on 299173db51. This revision moves the cap into
VllmConfig
and merges the startup check without changing admission: for this setup, its engine config leaves
max_num_active_seqs
unset at
--max-num-seqs 64
and lowers it to 102 at
--max-num-seqs 128
.
Not run: DFlash end to end on either runner.
Details
Root cause.
Both drafters run a separate fixed-width query pass. Context KV is precomputed from the target's hidden states into its own buffers, and each request's query rows go into buffers of
max_num_batched_tokens
rows:
DFlashSpeculator
/
DSparkSpeculator
on MRV2,
DFlashProposer.input_ids
on MRV1. The slots only enforced
num_reqs × query rows ≤ max_num_batched_tokens
. A request cap gives the same bound without spending target budget.
Why throughput gains more than 64/52.
On main, the 2–32 tokens left over split each new prefill into small chunks. Most steps then mix prefill into the decode batch and miss the FULL decode CUDA graph: ITL p50 is 169 ms on main vs 30 ms here.
Divisor.
num_lookahead_tokens
equals the draft pass's query rows per request: K for anchor-sampling DSpark, K + 1 for DFlash and fill-in DSpark. Each query row writes KV at a position that
allocate_slots(num_lookahead_tokens=...)
must cover. So it cannot fall below the query width without breaking draft KV allocation, and if it grows the cap only tightens. This also covers fill-in DSpark, whose old K − 1 charge did not bound its K + 1 query rows.
Where the cap lives.
Right after the startup check,
VllmConfig
lowers
scheduler_config.max_num_active_seqs
to the cap only when the cap is below the current limit, and logs why, e.g.
The dspark draft pass needs 5 query tokens per request within max_num_batched_tokens=512. Overriding max_num_active_seqs from 128 to 102.
The scheduler is unchanged. Only its admission check reads
max_num_active_seqs
; unlike
max_num_seqs
, it doesn't size runner buffers or CUDA graphs and isn't part of the config hash.
Startup check.
The existing
max_num_batched_tokens
check in
VllmConfig
now compares against
num_lookahead_tokens
instead of the draft slots.
num_lookahead_tokens
is at least every method's slots and covers the DFlash/DSpark draft pass, so the check still rejects a budget too small for one request's draft pass. It is slightly stricter than before: EAGLE, MTP and draft models now need a budget above K, and DFlash above K + 1, far below any practical budget.
MRV1.
DSpark is MRV2-only. MRV1 DFlash shares the scheduler and its drafter has the same structure, so it gets the same change. It is covered by unit tests only, not end to end.
Review changes.
Following
@TheEpicDolphin
's review:
the fix moved into
max_num_new_slots_for_drafting
, and the cap now applies on both runners instead of only MRV2;
the cap divides by
num_lookahead_tokens
, so anchor-sampling DSpark uses K rather than K + 1.
Not a duplicate.
[Bugfix] Separate target and draft scheduling budgets
#53080
(open, conflicting) replaces
max_num_new_slots_for_drafting
with a per-step draft budget for every method (+237/−77).
[Core] Separate DSpark scheduler input budgets
#52996
(open, conflicting) adds a DSpark-only budget charged K per request, which leaves DFlash over-charged.
[BUGFIX] Fix dflash batched token budget
#53970
resizes the drafter buffers; it is complementary.
AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the change, the tests, the test runs and this description.

…

…dget

The scheduler charges every request num_new_tokens plus
max_num_new_slots_for_drafting against max_num_batched_tokens: K for
DFlash and K - 1 for DSpark. Neither drafts in the target batch. Both
run a separate query pass whose rows go into max_num_batched_tokens-row
buffers, and the charge only kept that pass in bounds. A DSpark decode
with K = 5 costs 10 tokens instead of 6, so a budget of 512 runs at
most 51 requests.

Return 0 slots for DFlash and DSpark, and instead cap
max_num_active_seqs at max_num_batched_tokens // num_lookahead_tokens,
with a warning when that lowers it. num_lookahead_tokens is the draft
pass's query rows per request (K for anchor-sampling DSpark, K + 1 for
DFlash and fill-in DSpark), which its KV writes require it to cover. The startup check on
max_num_batched_tokens now compares against num_lookahead_tokens, which
is at least every method's draft slots, so it still rejects a budget
too small for one request's draft pass.

Purpose
Partial mitigation for
#52463
: the tie-break rotation added in
#47420
degrades prefix-cache locality for multi-turn / shared-prefix traffic under the internal DP load balancer. Consecutive turns of one conversation are tied decisions at low load, so they rotate across DP ranks and every turn misses the prefix its previous turn cached.
This PR remembers which engine served a prompt's first-block prefix (LRU of 16k entries, keyed on
cache_salt
+ LoRA id + first
block_size
prompt token ids) and prefers that engine
only when scores tie
:
Load-aware decisions unchanged — a lower-scored engine always wins.
Unrelated tied requests still rotate —
[Core][DP] Rotate load-balancer tie-break to avoid systematic engine bias
#47420
's fairness fix is preserved (regression-tested).
Explicit
data_parallel_rank
and late-interaction routing bypass affinity, unchanged.
Stale entries from elastic-EP scale-in are discarded; sub-block prompts (which cannot hit the cache) are exempt.
Test Plan
tests/v1/engine/test_dp_lb_prefix_affinity.py
— 8 CPU-only unit tests driving
get_core_engine_for_request
directly: session stickiness across turns, tied-unrelated rotation preserved, load-beats-affinity, sub-block exemption, cache_salt separation, explicit-rank bypass, scale-in staleness, LRU bound.
Hardware A/B on 8×H100 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, DP=4+EP,
--api-server-count 4
, fp8 KV, aiperf mooncake trace designed for 81.7% prefix reuse — full methodology in
[Bug][DP] Tie-break rotation from #47420 degrades prefix-cache locality for multi-turn traffic under internal DP LB
#52463
): identical runs, only this patch differs.
Test Result
Unit: 8/8 pass (run inside
vllm/vllm-openai:nightly
image).
Hardware A/B (prefix-cache hit rate, per-user output tok/s):

* hit rate unchanged while throughput moved — consistent with run-to-run variance at 160 requests/level, not a cache effect; happy to re-run if reviewers want more samples.
Known limitation (why this is a mitigation, not the full fix):
with
--api-server-count N
each frontend process has its own client and affinity map, and SO_REUSEPORT spreads one session's connections across processes — client-side affinity only sees its own process's requests (this bounds the c=1 recovery at 61.5% vs 81.6% measured on v0.23.0, a pre-
#47420
release — a version-level baseline, not a single-commit revert of
#47420
). The complete fix needs prefix-awareness at a shared layer (DP coordinator or a shared affinity table);
#52463
is the home for that design discussion.

vllm-project#47420
made tied load-balancing decisions rotate across engines to remove
a systematic tie-break bias. With prefix caching enabled this also rotates
consecutive turns of one conversation across DP ranks, so every turn
misses the prefix the previous turn left in KV cache. Measured on
DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DP=4+EP, 8xH100, multi-turn mooncake trace designed for
81.7% prefix reuse): hit rate 81.6% on pre-rotation v0.23.0, 8-53% on
current main, costing 2-13% per-user output throughput.

Remember which engine served a prompt's first-block prefix (LRU, keyed on
cache_salt + LoRA id + first block_size token ids) and prefer that engine
when scores tie. Load-aware decisions are unchanged, and unrelated tied
requests still rotate, preserving
vllm-project#47420
's fairness.

Purpose
When a large prefill is scheduled on only one DP engine, that engine performs a
much longer model iteration while the other engines wait for it to finish. This
creates uneven iteration times and delays ongoing decode requests.
This PR adds an optional adaptive prefill delayer. It coordinates large prefill
work onto the same engine steps across DP ranks, reducing iterations where one
rank is doing prefill while others are decoding. Decode continues while prefill
is delayed, with bounded fail-open and recovery behavior to guarantee progress.

Contributor
Overview
The DP ranks of a MoE engine step in lockstep. When any rank has prefill, the step becomes a long mixed (and, on some backends, eager) step for every rank. Agentic multi-turn traffic makes prefill frequent, so decode keeps getting interrupted.
--dp-prefill-delayer
(opt-in, default off) aligns prefill across the ranks and protects the decode steps after a prefill. It follows ATOM's PrefillDelayer.
Claims
Measured on a development branch with an earlier version of this change: DeepSeek-V4-Pro on 8x MI355X, DP8 attention + EP8, AgentX agentic workload, 1200 s runs, metrics over 300-1200 s, single runs per configuration.

The c128 rows use a later recipe with other changes; they differ only in the prefill policy. The no-delayer c128 row ran on a different node of the same type.
The trade-off is TTFT: prefill waits for the other ranks, and long prompts wait for alignment chunk by chunk.
Validation on this upstream branch is still to be added.
Validation
pytest tests/v1/core/test_prefill_delayer.py
: 14 passed (CPU). The tests cover each FIRE / HOLD rule and bound, the per-rank state, the scheduler gating and the config check.
pytest -m cpu_test tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py tests/v1/core/test_async_scheduler.py
and
tests/engine/test_arg_utils.py
: pass. They cover the changed
defer_prefills
expression with the delayer off.
pre-commit run --files <changed files>
: all hooks pass, mypy included.
No GPU runs on this branch yet.
Details
Protocol.
Once per engine step, each rank reports 6 ints in one CPU SUM all-reduce on the DP group: prefillable, pending prefill tokens (capped at
max_num_batched_tokens
), running decodes, KV usage >= 0.9, chunk in progress, prefill ran. Every rank then takes the same FIRE / HOLD decision for its next schedule.
Placement.
The all-reduce sits next to
_has_global_unfinished_reqs()
. Every rank reaches that point on every non-idle step (real, dummy and pause steps alike), which the existing DP state sync already relies on, so the extra collective cannot be skipped by one rank. The state resets at each DP wave boundary.
Rules (ATOM's), in order:
A step that ran prefill arms
--dp-prefill-delayer-protected-steps
(default 10) steps that HOLD while decodes run.
FIRE if no rank has prefill, no rank decodes, or KV usage is high.
FIRE after 200 held steps, or after 100 with a chunk in progress.
HOLD until all ranks have prefill.
FIRE when the pending tokens reach 0.9 x prefillable ranks x
max_num_batched_tokens
, or when the backlog stops growing for 10 steps.
HOLD scope.
HOLD defers all prefill compute, new requests and in-progress chunks, even on a rank without local decodes, so that ranks prefill together.
Interaction with
--prefill-schedule-interval
.
The delayer replaces it; setting both is an error.
Cost.
Off: none. On: one 6-int CPU all-reduce per step.
Not supported:
elastic EP and custom scheduler classes.
Relation to
[Perf] Add an adaptive prefill delayer for data-parallel serving
#51199
(cc
@kjiang249
). That PR coordinates releases through the DP coordinator (asynchronous, with acks and a 2-step lead); this one uses a synchronous per-step all-reduce in the engine loop and adds protected decode steps and a token fill target. We drove both decision functions in a CPU simulation of 8 lockstep ranks with agentic traffic:
[Perf] Add an adaptive prefill delayer for data-parallel serving
#51199
's all-ranks release rarely triggered; most of its releases came from its capacity and 30-pass fail-open bounds.
This delayer had 2-4x fewer mixed steps and about half the mean decode latency.
[Perf] Add an adaptive prefill delayer for data-parallel serving
#51199
had about 3x lower TTFT.
The two are complementary, and I am happy to merge efforts.
AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for this PR.

skill. (Mandatory for agents, optional for humans).

--dp-prefill-delayer (off by default) aligns prefill across the lockstep
ranks of a data-parallel MoE engine, following ATOM's PrefillDelayer: once
per engine step the ranks all-reduce a 6-int prefill state on the DP group
and all take the same FIRE / HOLD decision for the next step. A step that
ran prefill is followed by --dp-prefill-delayer-protected-steps (default 10)
decode-only steps; otherwise prefill waits until every rank has some and
the pending tokens fill 0.9 of the prefillable ranks' token budgets, with
bounds for no decode, KV usage, held steps (200, or 100 with a chunk in
progress) and a stalled backlog. The all-reduce runs where the existing DP
state sync runs, so every rank reaches it in the same steps. It replaces
--prefill-schedule-interval; setting both is an error.

Why
--prefill-schedule-interval
does not solve it here
The interval coordinates
when
the DP ranks may prefill: they share the step counter, so on off-cadence steps every rank defers prefill. It does not coordinate
whether
they prefill: each rank decides from its own queue and sees nothing of the other ranks. Under agentic load this still lets prefill reach most steps:
After a release step, a rank whose waiting queue did not fit the token budget (
prefill_capacity_bound
) stops throttling and prefills on every step until the queue drains. The check is local to the rank, but one prefilling rank makes the step mixed for all 8 ranks. With 90-130K-token prompts at c128, some rank is often in this state. This is our reading of the c128 result; we have not counted the mixed steps yet.
A cadence step runs whatever prefill each rank has, even one small chunk on one rank, and the other ranks pay a full mixed step for it.
The delayer adds the missing state exchange. Once per step the ranks all-reduce a few counters (pending prefill tokens, running decodes, KV pressure), and every rank takes the same decision. It fires when the pending tokens across the ranks reach about 90% of their budget, then keeps the next N steps decode-only.
Next steps
This PR is at an early stage. Our next goal is to lower TTFT, or at least bound it so that a TTFT SLA can be met:
A time-based bound: release when the oldest waiting prefill has waited longer than a configured budget in ms.
A sweep against interval 8 / 16 (with and without the long-prefill threshold) across concurrency, reported as throughput vs E2E-normalized interactivity and throughput vs TTFT.
A looser alignment is a first candidate. We tried releasing with 6-7 of 8 ranks ready and a shorter partial-chunk hold, on the current recipe and against the same-node default. At about the same throughput (-1.8% to +1.3%), TTFT went down 28-39% and the E2E-normalized p90 went up 29-42%, while the ITL-only p90 went down 15-24%.
Also related:
#54627
(just merged) has the same basic idea, holding prefill so that decode runs in longer stretches, but it applies only when data_parallel_size == 1. On MoE DP ranks it is a no-op. There, the existing cadence aligns when the ranks may prefill, but no rank sees the other ranks' queues. This PR adds that cross-rank state: one small all-reduce per step, so every rank takes the same prefill decision.

Contributor
Purpose
DeepSeek-V4.1's Engram tables are already MXFP8 (FP8 rows with one ue8m0 scale per 32 values) and
wkv
is an MXFP8 GEMM, but the lookup dequantizes each row to BF16, DP replicas all-gather those 512-byte rows layer by layer, and
wkv
quantizes them right back. This PR keeps rows packed from the host table to
wkv
.
Packed rows, direct MXFP8.
The lookup copies each row's 256 FP8 bytes and 8 scale bytes as they are, and one unpack kernel writes them in FlashInfer's MXFP8 activation layout (F8_128x4 scales).
wkv
takes them as a
QuantizedActivation
, so both the dequant and the requant are gone, and the output is bit-identical.
One all-to-all per prefill step.
EngramBatch
looks up every local Engram layer into one packed buffer and exchanges it with a single all-to-all, which sends each rank only its own tokens (264 instead of 512 bytes per head row, 1/DP of an all-gather), then unpacks all layers in one launch.
Peer exchange for decode.
Below 128 tokens per rank,
EngramPeerExchange
replaces the hash all-gather and the per-layer row all-gathers: ranks publish ids in symmetric memory, look up their head shard for every peer's tokens, and read their own tokens back from the peers after a barrier. All layers share one lookup and one unpack launch.
The batched path serves DP-sharded tables (
embedding_across_dp
without DP-shared memory) with TP = 1,
head_dim % 128 == 0
, no LoRA (it wraps
wkv
after construction), and a
wkv
kernel that takes F8_128x4 scales (reusing
can_fuse_query_quant
). The peer exchange also needs SM100, CPU offload, and 2/4/8 fully connected GPUs; without it every slot uses the all-to-all, which on DEP4 HBM tables at 1–127 tokens per rank is 19–58 us faster than the BF16 path. Everything else, including TP, DP-shared tables, single replicas and ROCm, keeps the existing BF16 path unchanged. Communication stays on the current stream and
wkv
still runs in
Engram.forward
.
Also changed along the way:
EngramBatch
is an
nn.Module
, so the peer exchange's pointer tables are model buffers that level-2 sleep restores.
fused_q_kv_rmsnorm_quant
and the Engram unpack kernel share the F8_128x4 scale offset and size helpers.
Kernel microbenchmark
The benchmarks, E2E runs and the first accuracy table were measured on
d593d7f
.
3724967
only drops paths that DEP + THP never takes and keeps its
wkv
outputs bitwise identical (see Test Result).
Engram only, two layers (lookup, exchange, and anything needed to reach the MXFP8
wkv
input), 4 x GB300 in one node. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash table sizes (24 heads x 16M rows, 94.4 GiB per layer) as DP-shared
/dev/shm
tables or private THP shards, uniform random ids rotating 3 sets, 256 MiB L2 flush per sample, full CUDA graph replay, median of 40 samples of the slowest rank, best of 2 rounds. Since this PR's output is already the
wkv
input, the BF16 columns include their activation quantization (17 us for decode, 203 us at 32K tokens).

Overview
With
dp_shared_memory
, node-local DP ranks share one registered
/dev/shm
mapping for the Engram host tables (2 layers x 94.4 GiB on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash). Lookups are random row reads and on GB200 they are bound by GPU TLB misses: the registered mapping uses 64K pages.
This PR allocates the shared table as host-NUMA cuMem instead, which the GPU maps with 2M pages. Rank 0 creates it and broadcasts a FABRIC handle; the other node-local DP ranks import and map it. Where FABRIC handles are unavailable (probed once: create + export), the existing
/dev/shm
path is used and logged. Rank 0 decides the backing and broadcasts it so every rank runs the same collectives. A mapping failure on any rank raises on all ranks.

sources.body:
Conversation
ivanium
commented
Sep 14, 2026
•
edited
Loading
Uh oh!
There was an error while loading.
Please reload this page

Copy link
Copy Markdown
Contributor
Purpose
Stacked on
#56227
(base branch
feat/dsv41-swa-bounded-replay
; the diff shows only this PR's three commits). DeepSeek-V4.1's layers past the last KV-source layer (21-39 on V4.1-Flash) own nothing but sliding-window KV: every later layer attends the compressed KV of the source layers, and only the last 128 tokens' window KV is read after prefill. This is DeepSeek's decoder-side SWA bounded replay: in prefill those layers run on each request's last 128 tokens only, cold prefills included, while layers 0-20 still run on every token. It is a deliberate approximation, not an equivalent reduction of work: the kept rows' window attention in layers 21-39 is bounded at the trailing window (the SWA kernels read no window KV below it), so the last token's hidden state is not bit-identical to a full prefill; the long-range context reaches it through the compressed KV. The accuracy runs below (gsm8k on TP4 and DP4, two passes each) and DSpark's unchanged acceptance length are what this rests on.
DeepseekV4Model
(
nvidia/model.py
): when the layers after the last KV source are all sliding-window and the configuration allows it, the forward is split into
_run_layers
up to the cut,
DecoderReplayLayers
for the rest, and the final mHC collapse. Otherwise the forward is unchanged and a warning names the reason.
DeepseekV41ModelState.prepare_attn
(
nvidia/model_state.py
): after the step's own metadata it builds the replay layers' batch from the same inputs: the replay rows (one Triton kernel fills the rows, the row-subset
InputBuffers
, its slot mappings and its replay start), attention metadata through metadata builders of its own (the runner's hold the batch's metadata past the forward) and, under piecewise graphs, the size of the replay layers' graph. Everything lives in persistent buffers because that graph reads them by address. The result is set on
DecoderReplayLayers.replay_batch
; it is None when nothing trims in an eager forward and under FULL graphs (uniform decode).
DecoderReplayLayers
(
decoder_replay_layers.py
): gathers the seven layer inputs by the rows, runs the layers under a copy of the forward context with the replay batch's attention metadata, slot mappings, padding mask, batch descriptor and DP metadata, and scatters the outputs back to full-batch rows. Under breakable piecewise graphs the replay is an eager break of the model graph: the layers run in a graph of their own (
ReplayCudaGraphs
, keyed by the replay batch's padded size) captured inside the model graph's capture of the same size. Only prefills trim, so a capture's dummy batch keeps all its rows and every capture size gets a replay graph of that size; at runtime the replay batch pads to the smallest capture size that fits, which therefore always exists.
Data parallelism: the replay layers' MoE collectives need every rank's token count, so the model state has the ranks agree in
prepare_attn
with one CPU all-reduce carrying whether each rank trims and its replay token count. Any rank trimming makes every rank replay on those counts; under graphs all ranks run the one replay graph size that fits the largest count.
DSpark (
dspark/speculator.py
): the drafter derives its context KV from the target's aux hidden states, which under decoder replay exist only for the last window of each request;
_context_rows
bounds the context KV writes to the drafter's own window.
Shared changes, none behavioral for other models:
AttentionGroup.make_metadata_builder
(a builder outside the group's own list),
prepare_inputs_to_capture
hands the model state the capture's real cudagraph mode (the default state treats PIECEWISE like NONE), and an eager break of a breakable capture may capture graphs of its own.
The decoder side stays off, with a warning, when the pipeline stage does not hold every layer after the last KV source, under sequence-parallel MoE, prefill context parallelism or microbatching, with an Engram layer after the cut, or with a drafter whose window is wider than the target's. DeepSeek-V4.1 turns sequence-parallel MoE on for EP with TP > 1 under DP, so under DP the decoder side runs with TP = 1 today.
No other open PR implements the decoder side of SWA replay;
#56227
is the encoder side this builds on.
Usage
Nothing to configure: with
#56227
and this PR, DeepSeek-V4.1 on model runner V2 replays on both sides by default, including under
--data-parallel-size > 1
with TP = 1.
--no-swa-bounded-replay
turns both sides off.
Test Plan
pytest tests/models/test_deepseek_v41_replay_batch.py tests/models/test_deepseek_v4_decoder_replay_layers.py \
  tests/v1/cudagraph/test_breakable_cudagraph.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dspark_context_rows.py
Accuracy:
deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
served on a GB200 node with
vllm serve
(default
FULL_AND_PIECEWISE
with breakable piecewise graphs), gsm8k (5-shot) run twice against the same server, pass 2 re-sending every prompt so each request is a full-prompt prefix hit, concurrency 512: TP4 (
--max-num-seqs 1024
) and DP4 x TP1 x EP4 (
--max-num-seqs 256
per rank). Baseline arms are
--no-swa-bounded-replay
on the same tree.
Test Result
Unit tests cover the replay rows and sub-batch fields (including prompt-logprobs requests, which keep every row, and the adaptive-verification query bound), the graph-size and DP agreement rules, an idle DP rank's dummy batch, gather/scatter with the indexer buffers, the replay graph against the eager path on a batch it never saw, nested breakable captures and the DSpark context rows; pre-commit and mypy are clean.
gsm8k, n=1319, 0 request errors in every pass, decoder replay engaged on every rank:
arm

[Model] Decoder-side SWA bounded replay for DeepSeek-V4.1
…
e8a0735
DeepSeek-V4.1's layers past the last KV-source layer (21-39 on V4.1-Flash) own nothing but sliding-window KV, so in prefill they only need each request's last window of tokens. DeepseekV41ModelState builds that batch in prepare_attn, right after the step's own metadata and from the same inputs: the replay rows, a row-subset InputBatch, attention metadata from metadata builders of its own and, under piecewise graphs, the size of the replay layers' graph, all in fixed buffers. DecoderReplayLayers gathers the layer inputs by the rows, runs the layers under a forward context of their own (attention metadata, slot mappings, padding mask, batch descriptor), eagerly or in a breakable graph captured inside the model graph's capture of the same size, and scatters the outputs back to full-batch rows. Only prefills trim, so a capture's dummy batch keeps all its rows and every capture size gets a replay graph of that size.

Shared changes: AttentionGroup.make_metadata_builder for a builder outside the group's own list; prepare_inputs_to_capture hands the model state the capture's real cudagraph mode (the default state treats PIECEWISE like NONE); an eager break of a breakable capture may capture graphs of its own.

The decoder side stays off, with a warning, when the pipeline stage does not hold every layer after the last KV source, when the replay batch cannot shrink per rank (sequence, data or prefill-context parallelism, microbatching), with an Engram layer after the cut, or with a drafter whose window is wider than the target's.

Co-authored-by: zjy0516 <riverclouds.zhu@qq.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Yifan Qiao <yifanqiao@inferact.ai>
[SpecDecode] Bound the DSpark drafter's context KV to its window
…
618e894
A DSpark drafter whose layers are all sliding-window attention can only
ever read the last `window` context positions of a request, so projecting
and inserting context KV for the rest of a long prefill chunk is wasted
work. Under the target's decoder-side SWA bounded replay those rows also
carry no real hidden state (the target never computed them), so
restricting the precompute to the window removes the garbage KV they
produced. It rides --swa-bounded-replay. Adaptive verification sizes the
leading verification requests on the GPU, but those are never trimmed,
so the row selection from the CPU query boundaries still holds.

The DFlash context-KV precompute gains a row-selection hook that keeps
every row by default; DSpark implements it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Yifan Qiao <yifanqiao@inferact.ai>
[Model] Run DeepSeek-V4.1 decoder-side SWA bounded replay under data …
…
d87ddc6
…parallelism

The replay layers' MoE collectives need every DP rank's token count, and the
replay batch shrinks per rank, so the decoder-side replay stayed off under
DP. DeepseekV41ModelState now has the ranks agree on their replay batches
where it builds them, in prepare_attn, which every rank calls every step:
one CPU all-reduce carries whether each rank trims and how many tokens its
replay layers would run on. Any rank trimming makes every rank replay on
those counts, which are the replay layers' DP metadata in eager mode; under
graphs all ranks run the one replay graph size that fits the largest count,
or the padded batch's when none trims. An idle rank's dummy batch trims like
a real one, so its rows fit whatever size was agreed.

Microbatching (DBO) joins sequence and prefill-context parallelism in the
unsupported list; it runs the model per microbatch, outside this agreement.

diff --git a/vllm/distributed/utils.py b/vllm/distributed/utils.py
index 3618361f2a66..010d517d4645 100644
--- a/vllm/distributed/utils.py
+++ b/vllm/distributed/utils.py
@@ -55,6 +55,70 @@ def ensure_divisibility(numerator, denominator):
     )
 
 
+# P2P tags [base, base + log2(group size) + 1] are reserved for cpu_all_reduce_.
+_CPU_ALL_REDUCE_TAG_BASE = 27100
+
+
+def cpu_all_reduce_(tensor: torch.Tensor, group: ProcessGroup) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """Low-latency in-place SUM all-reduce of a small CPU tensor over a gloo group.
+
+    Recursive doubling within power-of-two blocks, then one concurrent exchange
+    between blocks. Results are bitwise identical across ranks. Works with
+    stateless (unregistered) process groups.
+    """
+    world_size = group.size()
+    if world_size == 1:
+        return tensor
+    block_size = world_size & -world_size
+    num_blocks = world_size // block_size
+    if tensor.device.type != "cpu" or not tensor.is_contiguous():
+        torch.distributed.all_reduce(tensor, group=group)
+        return tensor
+
+    rank = group.rank()
+    tag = _CPU_ALL_REDUCE_TAG_BASE
+
+    # Recursive doubling within the block (peers stay in the aligned block).
+    if block_size > 1:
+        # This branch applies only to even world sizes.
+        scratch = torch.empty_like(tensor)
+        mask = 1
+        while mask < block_size:
+            peer = rank ^ mask
+            # Wait for both ops before touching either buffer.
+            recv_work = group.recv([scratch], peer, tag)
+            send_work = group.send([tensor], peer, tag)
+            recv_work.wait()
+            send_work.wait()
+            tensor.add_(scratch)
+            mask <<= 1
+            tag += 1
+
+    # Exchange block sums with the same lane in every other block at once.
+    if num_blocks > 1:
+        # This branch applies only when world_size is not a power of two.
+        lane, my_block = rank % block_size, rank // block_size
+        block_sums = [
+            tensor if b == my_block else torch.empty_like(tensor)
+            for b in range(num_blocks)
+        ]
+        works = []
+        for b, buf in enumerate(block_sums):
+            if b != my_block:
+                works.append(group.recv([buf], b * block_size + lane, tag))
+        for b in range(num_blocks):
+            if b != my_block:
+                works.append(group.send([tensor], b * block_size + lane, tag))
+        for work in works:
+            work.wait()
+        # Sum in block order so every rank computes the identical result.
+        total = block_sums[0]
+        for buf in block_sums[1:]:
+            total.add_(buf)
+        tensor.copy_(total)
+    return tensor
+
+

Summary
This PR pipelines direct NVLink dispatch using three shared-memory TMA buffers per dispatch warp.
Previously, a dispatch warp prepared tokens sequentially around remote S2G stores. With this change, the next token's hidden data, scale factors, metadata, and routing information are prefetched while previous remote stores remain in flight.
At steady state, the three buffers are used for:
A previous token whose remote S2G store may still be in flight.
The current token being sent to remote ranks.
The next token being prefetched from global memory.
Before recycling the oldest buffer,
tma_store_wait<1>()
reduces the number of outstanding store groups to one. This keeps buffer reuse safe without fully draining all remote stores between tokens.
The shared-memory calculation now accounts for all three staging buffers, and direct NVLink dispatch is limited to at most 14 dispatch warps. The non-NVLink path remains single-buffered.
Validation
Tested on 8 x NVIDIA H100 GPUs with direct NVLink dispatch.

v6
The multi-buffer TMA scheduling and matching shared-memory sizing appear consistent across NVLink and non-NVLink paths, with outstanding stores flushed before buffer reuse.
v4
The dispatch kernel switches from single per-warp staging (drained fully per token) to three round-robin staging TMA buffers per dispatch warp. While the current token's remote S2G/NVLink/RDMA store stays in flight, the next token's hidden/SF/metadata/routing is prefetched into the buffer whose previous use is the oldest outstanding store group (deterministically token_iter - 2 of 3, or none on a warm-up iteration); tma_store_wait<1>() retires that group before the buffer is overwritten, and the final barrier drains the last in-flight store. The host sizes per-warp smem by 3x (RDMA: 1x) and caps NVLink dispatch warps at 14, with the RDMA path remaining single-buffered and full-drained (unchanged behavior). Edge cases (first iteration, last token skipped, warps with no tokens, per-token global slot/counter writes) are all safe and unchanged. Measured on 8xH100 dispatch goes 250->280 GB/s, combine unchanged. Overall the change correctly and faithfully implements the PR as a pure pipelining/perf optimization on the previously single-buffered path.
v3
This PR pipelines direct NVLink dispatch by switching from double- to triple-buffered TMA staging (kNumDirectNVLinkTmaBuffers 2->3, kNumTmaBuffers 2->3 for the NVLink path), and refactoring the per-token body into a
prepare_token
lambda so the next token's hidden/SF/metadata/routing can be prefetched while the current token's remote S2G stores are in flight. The phase tracking was generalized from two scalars (phase_0/phase_1) to a
phases[kNumTmaBuffers]
array, and buffer indexing changed from bitmask (
& (kNumTmaBuffers-1)
) to modulo (
% kNumTmaBuffers
) to support 3 (non-power-of-two) buffers. The host-side shared-memory computation already multiplies by num_tma_buffers and caps direct NVLink dispatch at 14 warps.
Correctness analysis (all verified sound):
Buffer-reuse safety: In steady state, entering iteration N up to 2 store groups (iters N-2, N-1) are outstanding.
tma_store_wait<1>()
retires iter N-2's store (which read buffer (N-2)%3 == (N+1)%3) before prepare_token(N+1) writes into that same buffer. This correctly matches the recycled buffer to the just-retired store group, so triple buffering is safe.
Per-buffer mbarrier phases persist across reuse (buffer b used at iters b, b+3, ...), and
phases[]
is zero-initialized; flip semantics are preserved.
The buffer indexing change to
% kNumTmaBuffers
is applied consistently in both prepare_token and the main loop and is required because 3 is not a power of two.
The NVLink prefetch (prepare_token for the next token) is issued before awaiting the current buffer's load arrival, correctly overlapping the next token's G2S load with the current token's remote S2G store; it targets a distinct buffer with an independent mbarrier so there is no cross-buffer hazard.
Non-NVLink path stays single-buffered (kNumTmaBuffers=1) and keeps a full
tma_store_wait()
drain before recycling; behavior is unchanged. Startup/drain edges (num_tokens <= 1, first iteration with no outstanding stores) are handled by the
next_token_idx < num_tokens
guards.
Host/device consistency: the smem divisor in dispatch.hpp accounts for num_tma_buffers=3 and matches the device-side kNumTmaBuffers.

What
Adds
tests/test_speculative_sampling_exactness.py
(plus a 7-line
tests/conftest.py
import shim, removable once packaging or a root conftest lands) — 8 CPU-only tests for the exactness ("lossless") guarantee of the rejection sampler:
Lossless theorem (statistical):
with proposals drawn from the declared
draft_probs
, the committed token at every position follows the target distribution — chi-square against an independent float64 reference, 20,000 rounds through
verify_draft_tokens
, thresholds set at ~1e-9 per-assert false-fail so the suite passes for any RNG stream (the fixed seed only makes failures reproducible).
Negative control:
proposals drawn from a distribution other than the declared
draft_probs
must be rejected (chi-square > 64; analytic non-centrality ~356, recomputed in-test so future edits cannot silently destroy its power). A distribution test that has never rejected anything proves nothing — and this is exactly the bug class of
Draft sampling uses a different distribution than speculative rejection
#31
.
Draft sampling uses a different distribution than speculative rejection
#31
regression (deterministic,
xfail(strict=True)
):
seed-matched equivalence between
sample_tokens
and sampling from the distribution
logits_to_probs
feeds to rejection. Currently xfails because of
Draft sampling uses a different distribution than speculative rejection
#31
(~1e-3 mismatch rate over 100k draws, deterministic for any seed). When the fix lands, the strict marker turns the XPASS into a reminder to delete it, arming the guard — happy to remove the marker on rebase if the fix merges first.
Deterministic units:
logits_to_probs
vs an independent float64 reference (catches precision regressions the statistical tests are numerically blind to), greedy argmax-chain accept/reject, stop-token truncation semantics,
sample_residual
zero/near-zero-mass fallback (seed-matched to the target distribution), and the zero-draft path.
Why
Exactness is the core claim of speculative decoding, and
#31
showed it can silently break; the fix in
#30
ships without a regression test. vLLM has maintained the same style of statistical test for its rejection sampler for years (
test_rejection_sampling_approximates_target_distribution
).
Verification
Pinned environment (torch 2.9.1 CPU, transformers 5.10.2; Python 3.10 and 3.12):

→

— the evaluator-dependent tests skip via
importorskip
instead of failing at collection.

BASS: Batched Attention-optimized Speculative Sampling



Haifeng Qian

  
Sujan Kumar Gonugondla

  
Sungsoo Ha

  
Mingyue Shang

  
Sanjay Krishna Gouda

  
Ramesh Nallapati

  
Sudipta Sengupta

  
Xiaofei Ma

  
Anoop Deoras



Abstract
 

Speculative decoding has emerged as a powerful method to improve latency and throughput in hosting large language models.
However, most existing implementations focus on generating a single sequence.
Real-world generative AI applications often require multiple responses and how to perform speculative decoding in a batched setting while preserving its latency benefits poses non-trivial challenges.
This paper describes a system of batched speculative decoding that sets a new state of the art in multi-sequence generation latency and that demonstrates superior GPU utilization as well as quality of generations within a time budget.
For example, for a 7.8B-size model on a single A100 GPU and with a batch size of 8, each sequence is generated at an average speed of 5.8ms per token, the overall throughput being 1.1K tokens per second.
These results represent state-of-the-art latency and a 2.15×\times speed-up over optimized regular decoding.
Within a time budget that regular decoding does not finish, our system is able to generate sequences with HumanEval Pass@First of 43% and Pass@All of 61%, far exceeding what’s feasible with single-sequence speculative decoding.
Our peak GPU utilization during decoding reaches as high as 15.8%, more than 3×\times the highest of that of regular decoding and around 10×\times of single-sequence speculative decoding.
 





**footnotetext: Equal contribution.
1AWS AI Labs.
2AWS NGDE.
3Amazon AGI (work done at AWS).
Correspondence to: Haifeng Qian <qianhf@amazon.com>, Sujan Kumar Gonugondla <gsujan@amazon.com>.


1 Introduction




In recent years, generative large language models (LLMs) have rapidly gained popularity due to their ability to generalize across a wide variety of tasks. These models are increasingly deployed commercially for applications such as coding assistants, writing aids, conversational agents, search and summarization tools and more. The accuracy performance of LLMs has been shown to scale with model size, with larger models demonstrating improved capabilities Kaplan et al. (2020). However, this improvement comes at the cost of greater latency during inference and increased computational requirements.


Figure 1: Comparing latency and GPU utilization of auto-regressive regular decoding (RD), single-sequence speculative decoding (SD) and our BASS method on two models. RD and BASS are measured with exponentially increasing batch sizes (BS).




Most popular LLMs are transformer-based decoder models. The inference speed of these models is often limited by memory bandwidth on typical hardware like GPUs. This is because GPUs tend to have much higher compute throughput relative to memory bandwidth. The auto-regressive decoding process of these models, where each output token is generated sequentially conditioned on previous tokens, means the entire model parameters need to be fetched from memory for each generated token. This sequential nature prevents parallelization during inference, resulting in under-utilization of available compute resources. For example, for both models in Figure 1, single-sequence regular decoding utilizes only 0.4% of GPU FLOPS.




To improve GPU utilization, batching multiple sequences is often employed to amortize the memory I/O costs across a batch and thereby utilize more FLOPS per memory I/O. However, large batch sizes are needed to effective utilize GPU compute, resulting in higher latency for individual sequences that are batched as well as bigger memory footprints. With larger model sizes, memory bottleneck becomes a challenge and limits allowable batch sizes.
In Figure 1 for example, the highest GPU utilization by batched regular coding is only 4.8% before going out-of-memory.




Speculative decoding has emerged as an effective approach to improve latency of LLMs by increasing GPU utilization. The key idea is to draft a few tokens (typically by using a smaller LLM) and verify their correctness with the main LLM. By processing the draft tokens in parallel, speculative decoding amortizes the memory I/O of model parameters across the tokens. Despite its advantages, speculative decoding has limitations: It processes a single sequence at a time, restricting the parallelism to the number of draft tokens. This caps the potential GPU utilization improvements.




To address this, we present Batched Attention-optimized Speculative Sampling (BASS) – a parallel speculative decoder that handles multiple sequences simultaneously.
BASS increases GPU utilization by parallelism across both the batch dimension and the draft-token dimension.
We implement customized CUDA kernels to handle ragged tensors during attention calculation, which are a challenge posed by batched speculative decoding, and design a heuristic to dynamically adjust draft length for each step.
As illustrated in Figure 1, BASS achieves latency and GPU utilization that are substantially improved from prior regular and speculative decoders.
By comprehensive experiments on three different models including CodeGen and OPT, we study these trends as well as accuracy benefits of BASS.
We study the impact of draft model design on overall system performance as well as that of algorithmic choices in attention kernels and draft lengths.
BASS is applicable to both batch generation from a same prompt and batch generation from a set of different prompts.




2 Background



2.1 Inference with LLMs


Figure 2: (a) Inference steps in regular decoding of an LLM. (b) Operations in multi-head attention.




This paper focuses on transformer-based Vaswani et al. (2017) decoder-only generative LLMs. The standard inference of these LLMs can be divided into two phases:
(a) context encoding (prefill) phase where the input prompt is processed in parallel to encode contextual information, and
(b) incremental decoding phase where the model auto-regressively generates output tokens one by one based on the encoded context (Figure 2(a)).




Consider a decoder-only transformer Radford et al. (2019) architecture with alternatively stacked feed-forward network layers and attention layers. In the attention mechanism (Figure 2(b)), key (kik_{i}), value (viv_{i}), and query (qiq_{i}) vectors are first computed by projecting the token embeddings for each position ii. The queries are then used to calculate the relevance of the current token with past positions, by estimating their correlation with the past keys.




During the context encoding phase, all prompt tokens are processed in parallel. The attention keys and values for all context tokens (KK and VV tensors) are cached during this phase. This phase exhibits high GPU utilization.




The incremental decoding phase is bottlenecked by memory I/O from repeated fetching of model parameters and the KV cache as each output token is decoded.
This phase is typically the dominant portion of inference time and exhibits low GPU utilization.
It is the focus of our optimizations.




2.2 Speculative decoding




Speculative decoding Stern et al. (2018); Xia et al. (2022); Leviathan et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023) is a popular technique to reduce latency of LLM inference. As illustrated in Figure 3, the idea is to use a small draft model to generate kk draft tokens. They are then processed by the main model as incremental context encoding to decide which draft tokens to accept.


Figure 3: Standard speculative decoding. The draft model (Draft M) generates kk draft tokens auto-regressively, which are then processed by the main model (M) in parallel to verify correctness.




The number of draft tokens to accept is decided based on the probabilities of generating these tokens according to the main and draft models. In the case of rejection, a corrected token is sampled from the outputs of the main model. Overall, this decision process is stochastic and is designed to be equivalent to sampling from the main model’s distribution Leviathan et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023). For example, we may accept the first five tokens, correct the sixth token, and then generate new draft tokens from the seventh position.




Latency benefit comes from the higher GPU utilization associated with incremental context encoding rather than auto-regressive decoding. More than 2×\times latency reduction has been reported in literature Leviathan et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023).


2.2.1 Limitations of speculative decoding




A major limitation of speculative decoding is that batch size of the main model’s generation
is preferably just 1, which is the setting in most existing works. It is straightforward to see why. In a naive implementation with batch size more than 1, we stop accepting tokens at the first reject position in the batch and hence lose some latency benefit. For illustration, let’s make a simplistic assumption that each token generated by the draft model has an independent chance pp of getting accepted, then the number of output tokens per draft has a geometric distribution with an expected value of 1/(1−p)1/(1-p). For example, if p=80p=80%, then on average the decoding process moves forward by 5 tokens per draft. With a batch size of bb, the probability of acceptance per position becomes pbp^{b}. For a batch size of five as an example, the probability of acceptance per position becomes 33% and on average the decoding process moves forward by merely 1.5 tokens per draft, and we have lost most, if not all, of the latency benefit.




To retain the latency benefit with b>1b>1, we need to accept variable numbers of draft tokens across a batch.
This poses challenges that no prior work has addressed efficiently and the existing systems remain single-sequence inference.






3 Batched Attention-optimized Speculative Sampling




Batched Attention-optimized Speculative Sampling (BASS) extends speculative decoding by enabling batch processing across multiple sequences. While speculative sampling improves GPU utilization for a single sequence, parallelism is limited to the small number of draft tokens per sequence (typically 5-10). Batching sequences with speculative decoding can further maximize GPU usage. To fully realize these benefits, specialized tensor manipulations and CUDA kernels are required.



3.1 Challenges with batching




One challenge with batched speculative decoding stems from the uncertainty in the numbers of acceptable draft tokens for each sequence, which vary across the batch.
LLM inference kernels are designed to handle regular shaped tensors, primarily driven by CUDA restrictions.
If we enforce a uniform sequence length across the batch, that would result in less accepted draft tokens and in diminishing benefits as discussed in Section 2.2.1.




In order to maintain the performance gains of speculative sampling, we need to be able to accept variable numbers of tokens across the batch.
This will result in variable sequence lengths across the batch and consequently ragged-shape KK and VV tensors.
In particular, this will affect the computations in the attention layer where we may not be able to batch the operations into a single kernel.
Handling this effectively needs careful design considerations.




Another challenge is the choice of draft lengths.
Although prior experimental systems tend to use a fixed draft length, real-life deployment requires adaptive draft lengths because different prompts may lead to different degrees of alignment between draft and main models during generation and hence different optimal draft lengths.
For efficient incremental context encoding by the main model, we need to choose a uniform draft length across the batch at each step, and this decision needs to balance the needs of the multiple sequences.




3.2 Proposed method


Figure 4: Attention calculation in BASS: (a) Attention compute flow, (b) BASS-PAD launches one kernel for QK GEMM and one kernel for PV GEMM by padding the KK, VV and PP tensors to the maximum sequence length across the batch, and (c) BASS-SPLIT launches one kernel per sequence and thereby accommodates variable sequence lengths.




The attention computation flow, illustrated in Figure 4(a), involves a GEMM11
 1
 
 
 
 General matrix multiplication (GEMM). operation between the query tensor QQ of the current tokens and the key tensor KK of all tokens processed so far, a softmax operation that outputs P=softmax⁡(QT​K/c)P=\mathrm{softmax}(Q^{T}K/c), and another GEMM operation between PP and value tensor VV of all tokens processed so far.
There are three ragged tensors, KK, VV and PP.
We propose two variants: BASS-PAD and BASS-SPLIT as illustrated in Figure 4(b) and Figure 4(c) respectively.
They implement the two GEMMs differently and share the same softmax operation: we simply launch separate softmax kernels, one for each sequence.




In the BASS-PAD approach, we pad the KK, VV and PP tensors along the sequence length dimension to match the longest sequence of the batch and use the padded tensors for computations.
We assign zero probabilities for the padded tokens in PP.
BASS-PAD does not incur additional cost of launching kernels, but we waste some compute to perform dummy computations with the padded elements.




The BASS-SPLIT approach is derived from the insight that attention operation is not associated with any model parameters and therefore applying batching to attention has no benefit of reducing the amount of GPU memory reads.
In this approach, we break up the KQ GEMM and the PV GEMM into smaller per-sequence kernels, so that we can handle the variable sequence-length dimension in KK, VV and PP tensors, as shown in Figure 4(c).
Note that these separate kernels can be launched and executed in parallel.
Since there is no sharing of memory reads among these separate kernels, the only extra cost that we pay is the cost of launching them.
BASS-SPLIT does not waste any compute.




BASS-PAD and BASS-SPLIT apply to both the main and the draft models and apply to both token generation and incremental context encoding. With either approach, we can now let each sequence proceed at its own pace according to its own reject points and let sequences in the batch have different lengths.




Note that other steps, including the feed-forward network, the KQV projection layer, and the projection layer at end of attention, all remain the same and remain regularly batched to share memory reads of model parameters.




The comparison between BASS-PAD and BASS-SPLIT depends on the application scenario.
We find BASS-PAD more attractive when the sequence lengths are closer to each other and BASS-SPLIT more favorable when the sequence lengths across batch vary by a large margin.
Most results in Section 4 are based on BASS-PAD and their comparison results are in Section 4.6.


Algorithm 1 A heuristic to adjust draft length




 
 
 ldraft←l0l_{\text{draft}}\leftarrow l_{0}




 
 
 s←s\leftarrow 0




 
 
 for each speculative decoding step do




 
 
   x1,⋯,xb←x_{1},\cdots,x_{b}\leftarrow numbers of accepted tokens




 
 
   if max⁡(x1,⋯,xb)=ldraft\max\left(x_{1},\cdots,x_{b}\right)=l_{\text{draft}} then




 
 
    ldraft←min⁡(ldraft+lincre,llimit)l_{\text{draft}}\leftarrow\min\left(l_{\text{draft}}+l_{\text{incre}},l_{\text{limit}}\right)




 
 
    s←s\leftarrow 0




 
 
   else



 
 
    ldraft←ldraft−⌈ldraft/lmod⌉−sl_{\text{draft}}\leftarrow l_{\text{draft}}-\lceil l_{\text{draft}}/l_{\text{mod}}\rceil-s




 
 
    ldraft←max⁡(1,x1,⋯,xb,ldraft)l_{\text{draft}}\leftarrow\max\left(1,x_{1},\cdots,x_{b},l_{\text{draft}}\right)




 
 
    s←s\leftarrow 1

Algorithm 1 describes the heuristic that we use to dynamically adjust draft lengths.
The rationale is to increase draft length when at least one sequence has accepted all draft tokens in the last speculative decoding step and to decrease it otherwise.
The speed of decrease is larger when the current draft length is larger and when it is a consecutive step of decrease.
However, the next draft length is never decreased to be less than the max number of accepted tokens in the batch.
We empirically chose the parameters of l0=7l_{0}=7, lincre=2l_{\text{incre}}=2, lmod=10l_{\text{mod}}=10 and llimit=32l_{\text{limit}}=32.
Comparisons against constant draft lengths are in Section 4.6.




The degree of alignment between draft and main models varies across prompts, across different sequences from the same prompt, and also within the same sequence. When generating commonly used sentences or boilerplate code for example, the alignment tends to be strong and the optimal draft length is long. When generating uncommon sentences or novel code segments, the alignment tends to be weak and the optimal draft length is short. The effect of Algorithm 1 versus a fixed draft length is to dynamically get closer to the optimal draft length in both scenarios, so that the system generates longer drafts where possible yet does not waste compute to generate throw-away tokens.





4 Experiments




In this section we demonstrate the benefits of BASS over batched auto-regressive regular decoding (RD) and single-sequence speculative decoding.

4.1 Setup




Inference setup and CUDA kernels:
All experiments throughout this paper are conducted on a single A100 GPU with 40GB memory.
All inference runs, except for the “vLLM” rows in Tables 1 and 2, use a modified version of DeepSpeed22
 2
 
 
 
 https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed (DS), including both regular decoding and BASS runs.
As can be seen in the tables, the regular decoding latencies are at the state of the art and comparable to those reported in Aminabadi et al. (2022); Yao et al. (2022) for both FP16 and INT8.
The vLLM runs use the latest vLLM version33
 3
 
 
 
 https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm (v0.3.0) and all sequences start immediately and hence result in the best possible latencies.
Our modifications to DeepSpeed include:


• 



Kernels for quantizing both weights and activations to INT8 for all linear layers. We use CUTLASS44
 4
 
 
 
 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass INT8→\rightarrowINT32 kernels for GEMM calls and modify them and other layers to fuse quantization and de-quantization operators.


• 



Kernels for attention calculations to address the ragged-tensor challenge in batched speculative decoding without sacrificing latency, as discussed in Section 3.






Models and tasks: We report experimental results on three main models with their respective draft models and tasks55
 5
 
 
 
 While the three tasks are the scenario of batch generation from a same prompt, please note that BASS is also applicable to batch generation from a set of different prompts.:


• 



OPT 13B as the main model and OPT 125M or 350M as the draft model Zhang et al. (2022).
Following the same experimental setting as Chen et al. (2023), we use the XSum task with 11,334 test examples Narayan et al. (2018), use 1-shot prompting, generate 128 tokens per sequence, and use ROUGE-2 Lin (2004) as the metric to verify accuracy.


• 



CodeGen-Mono 16B as the main model and CodeGen-Mono 350M as the draft model.
We use the HumanEval task with 164 examples and use the Pass@KK accuracy metric Chen et al. (2021),
and we generate 256 tokens for each sequence.


• 



A 7.8B model trained on text and code as the main model and one of three draft models with sizes 310M, 510M and 1B.
We again use the HumanEval task.






Latency metrics: We use the metric of per-token latency for each generated sequence 66
 6
 
 
 
 It is important to note that we do not divide latency by batch size, which was done in some papers, e.g., Su et al. (2023). Fundamentally, our definition is a latency metric while the definition in Su et al. (2023) is a throughput metric. With our definition, per token latency increases as the batch size increases because the amount of FLOPS during the per token latency is multiplied by batch size, and this applies to both regular decoding and speculative decoding..
For regular decoding, this value is the same across a batch.
For speculative decoding, it varies within a batch and therefore we report three metrics: per-token latency of the first finished sequence in a batch, per-token latency of the last finished sequence in a batch, and per-token latency averaged across a batch, where each of the three is then averaged across examples in a task dataset.




4.2 Performance on summarization




Table 1 shows the accuracy and latency results of the OPT 13B model on the summarization task of the XSum dataset, with OPT 125M as the draft model.
As expected, the results suggest neutral accuracy between regular decoding and speculative decoding, while speculative decoding provides up to 2.81×\times speed up for finishing the first sequence and up to 2.34×\times speed up on average for all sequences.
In a real-life application, and particularly in the scenario of generating multiple sequences for the same prompt, we can respond to the user as soon as the first sequence finishes while the other additional recommendations continue to generate.
Therefore, speeding up the first sequence by 2.05×\times–2.81×\times implies a significant improvement in user-perceived latency.




The latency divergence between the first and last finished sequences increases with batch size. However, the last sequence latency is not as important in a real-life application because, when generating multiple sequences for the same prompt, we can simply choose a cut-off latency limit and return, e.g., five finished sequences out of a batch of eight.

4.5 Benefits of batched speculative decoding




Figure 5 emulates a real-life application scenario where a service returns code recommendations to a user within a time budget. One of the recommendations is first displayed and the user has the option to flip through others. Ranking (here simply mean-logP based) is applied to pick the first displayed one. The Pass@First metric is the probability that the first displayed recommendation solves the problem correctly. The Pass@Finished metric is the probability that at least one of the finished recommendations within the time budget solves the problem correctly. These two metrics together quantify the accuracy quality of the service.




Figure 5 uses an end-to-end time budget of 2.5 seconds to generate 256-long sequences for any given prompt from HumanEval.
According to Table 3, regular decoding under any setting would be unable to finish before time runs out, while single-sequence speculative decoding is able to return one recommendation and its Pass@First and Pass@Finished are the same and correspond to the left end point of the curves.
With BASS and as the batch size increases, Pass@Finished is increased up to 61% and Pass@First is increased up to 43% with a simple ranking strategy using model confidence of mean-logP value.
Both numbers are substantially higher than the mid-thirties accuracy by single-sequence speculative decoding.
A real-life application would use a domain-specific stopping criteria instead of a fixed length and a more sophisticated ranking method, but the relative comparisons among the competing methods are as captured by Figure 5 and BASS is clearly superior.


Figure 5: A 7.8B code model’s accuracy on HumanEval with BASS, within a time budget of 2.5 seconds. tt is temperature.




4.6 Ablation studies




In Table 6, we compare latency when certain alternative implementation choices are used.
With BASS-SPLIT, we launch per-sequence kernels to handle ragged tensors as illustrated in Figure 4(c).
The results suggest that the cost of launching more CUDA kernels in BASS-SPLIT out-weights the cost of wasted compute in BASS-PAD.
Note that this relation is task dependent and may change when the sequence lengths across a batch vary by a large margin.
For example, when applied on tasks of batch generation from a set of different prompts, the advantages of BASS-SPLIT could out-weights the cost.
With “fixed draft size”, we use a constant draft length instead of Algorithm 1 that dynamically modifies draft length.
The results suggest that both the efficient attention calculation and the draft-length heuristic are important to the performance of BASS.

5 Related Work




Efficient inference of LLMs has been a popular research topic in recent years.
Model quantization techniques Yao et al. (2022); Lin et al. (2023); Frantar et al. (2022); Kuzmin et al. (2022) employ lower-precision representations for model parameters (e.g., INT8, INT4, FP8) without significantly compromising accuracy. Pruning Frantar and Alistarh (2023) reduces memory footprints via sparsity.
Sparse attention techniques (Beltagy et al., 2020; Child et al., 2019) limit the number of tokens to attend to in order to reduce the complexity of attention layers, and thereby extend the maximum allowable sequence length.




Since its introduction, speculative decoding has seen numerous variations and improvements. Some proposals take a draft-model-free approach, by using an n-gram model to predict draft tokens Fu et al. (2023), or by using the model embedding to predict drafts Cai et al. (2024); Li et al. (2024). SpecInfer Miao et al. (2023) uses a draft tree to generate and organize multiple drafts for the main-model sequence in order to maximize the number of tokens accepted per step. Su et al. (2023) study the relation between batch size and the optimal fixed draft length for max throughput; it is however based on a primitive prototype implementation: rejected draft tokens are masked rather than discarded, which achieve sequence lengths that are uniform across a batch yet are unnecessarily large and inefficient.
The above works on speculative decoding are orthogonal to the discussions and ideas in this paper and can be combined. The conclusion presented in Su et al. (2023) may change with the kernel implementations in this paper.




6 Conclusion




This paper presents Batched Attention-optimized Speculative Sampling (BASS), a system that advances the state of the art in fast multi-sequence generation by LLMs.
By addressing the unique challenges of extending speculative decoding to batched inference without sacrificing latency, we demonstrate superior latency, GPU utilization as well as accuracy of generations within a time limit.




7 Limitations




This work, while advancing the state of the art, does not solve the efficient inference challenge of LLMs.
For example, GPU utilization during the context encoding phase of LLM inference can be over 70% in our system, while the best achievable utilization during the incremental decoding phase is 15.8% in this paper.
Although this is already significantly better than previous works, there is clearly substantial room to innovate and improve.




8 Ethical Impact




This work aims to increase the efficiency of deploying LLMs by utilizing the compute resources efficiently.
It can reduce carbon emissions associated with LLM deployment.
Additionally, driving down infrastructure costs can potentially encourage broader LLM adoption.
Impact of increased LLM usage on the society and associated risks are difficult to forecast.

Appendix A Appendix



A.1 Quantization schemes and mechanisms




This section describes the quantization schemes and kernels used for INT8 inference. Since granular assignment of precision improves the accuracy of quantized models, we assign the quantization ranges to the smallest granularity that allows us to compute the matrix multiplications in integer arithmetic, i.e., the granularity is set to the inner-product dimension. This translates to per-channel quantization for weights, dynamic per-token quantization for activation, and dynamic per-head and per-token quantization for keys, queries, and values.




To mitigate the overheads associated with quantize and dequantize operations in the inference pipeline on a GPU, we have employed kernel fusion techniques as shown in Figure 6. This involves amalgamating multiple operations to minimize CUDA kernel calls and memory fetches, thereby minimizing computation time.




Dynamic quantization can incur substantial overheads unless it is integrated with other operations in the inference pipeline. We fuse the quantize operation with layer-norm, GeLU, and transpose operations across the network. This approach eliminates the need for redundant memory reads, for example, reading the same data for layer-norm and quantization separately.




We use CUTLASS
INT8 GEMM kernels to fuse the dequantize operation and other element-wise computations, such as bias and residual additions with the GEMM operations. To optimize performance for small batch sizes, we adopt a strategy of pre-multiplying the weights and activation scales during the activation quantization operation, and subsequently retrieving them during the epilogue phase of the GEMM operations. The resulting fused GEMM blocks yield floating-point precision outputs, namely FP16, BF16 or FP32, depending on the selected format.


Figure 6: Inference data-flow with quantization




A.2 Draft model choice and training




For a draft model to be effective we need to maximize the number of tokens accepted by the main model while maintaining low per-token latency. Given the requirement, we have investigated architecture selection and observed that, at a fixed parameter count, having more attention heads (wider model) is better than having more layers with fewer attention heads (deeper model) since we have similar representation capabilities with wider-but-shallow models as narrow-but-deep models but at a much lower latency. We summarize the draft model architecture choices in Table 4.




We trained each of these draft models using the same data for the main model with a context size of 2048 and a global 512 batch size across 8 servers each with 8 40GB Nvidia A100 GPUs. This translates to approximately 1 million tokens per batch. Using a learning rate of 3.5×10−43.5\times 10^{-4} we train for 300k steps.
We use AdamW optimizer Kingma and Ba (2014) with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, and ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}. The warm-up steps were set to 2000, and a cosine annealing learning rate schedule was employed after reaching the peak learning rate.
The minimum learning rate was set to 10% of the peak learning rate.
We use BF16 Kalamkar et al. (2019) precision and set gradient clipping to 1.0 to enhance training stability.

CacheRoute: Planned Prefix-Affinity Routing

for Large-Scale LLM Serving



Huang Cheng

Affiliation: Meta, Menlo Park, California, USA

Email: huangcheng@meta.com


August 2026


Abstract
 

Prefix caching avoids prefill only when a repeated request returns to a server that still holds the prefix KV. Cache-blind balancing disperses that reuse; fixed affinity preserves it but can overload a server. CacheRoute resolves this tradeoff with a periodic routing plan. It admits high-rate keys to a stable warm set and places their assignments by expected load. Hot keys may use more than one destination, although every key in our primary semi-synthetic aggregate uses exactly one. On Llama-3.3-70B in fp8 across 60 H100 GPUs, CacheRoute sustains ±11176\!\pm\!11 QPS at a 3.5-s p99 SLO, 2.3×2.3\times the strongest of five baselines. Served KV-cache hit rate rises from ±1.3%64.1\!\pm\!1.3\% under cache-blind balancing to ±0.5%93.2\!\pm\!0.5\%. A second semi-synthetic aggregate and controlled 8B and burst experiments separate the effects of affinity and placement. Two 32B workloads provide the counterexamples: when affinity recovers too little KV work, its residual load skew reduces or erases the improvement. We therefore recommend gating any deployment with a shadow replay rather than enabling affinity from workload statistics alone.
 




Keywords: LLM serving; prefix caching; request routing; request scheduling.



1 Introduction




Prefix caching is now standard in LLM serving engines [Kwon et al.(2023), Zheng et al.(2024)], but the cache cannot control where a request lands. A cache-blind balancer spreads a recurring prefix across many destinations and lengthens the return time to each cache. Pinning a key to one destination restores locality, but maps key skew directly onto server queues. Cache-aware routers instead react to current cache and load state [Srivatsa et al.(2024), Yuan et al.(2026)]; once a destination fills, however, spilling the next request also forfeits the warm prefix.




This problem arises in multi-tenant conversational assistants—for example, customer-support chatbots—where each business carries a stable, reusable context across a multi-turn conversation. Such skewed, prefix-reusing serving is common across LLM serving systems and not specific to any one provider. A stable per-business context recurs across conversations, while the default balancer often sends successive requests to different model servers. Request rates also vary sharply across businesses, which rules out simple stickiness. The router must keep reusable prefixes local without creating a server whose queue sets the fleet-wide p99.




CacheRoute builds a routing table from measured per-key rates. It admits the highest-rate keys under a warm-prefix slot allocation, gives an overloaded key enough destinations to cap its expected load per destination, and places the resulting assignments with longest-processing-time-first (LPT) list scheduling. Unadmitted traffic falls back to cache-blind power-of-two choices. The table remains fixed for a control interval, favoring cache stability over per-request remapping.




Assignment and replication play different roles. In the primary distribution, even the hottest key falls below the single-destination load target; every assignment count is one. The 70B result therefore measures planned single-copy affinity, top-rate admission, and balanced placement. Only the controlled 8B experiments inject keys hot enough to exercise replication.




The main experiment serves Llama-3.3-70B in fp8 on 30 tensor-parallel-2 destinations (60 H100 GPUs). Across five paired runs, CacheRoute sustains ±11176\!\pm\!11 QPS at p99≤3.5\leq 3.5 s; the strongest baseline, Preble, sustains ±1176\!\pm\!11 QPS. At 100 offered QPS, CacheRoute’s p99 is 1.8 s, compared with 3.8–8.5 s for the five baselines. On a second distribution, the advantage is 1.6×1.6\times at the wider active set. The 8B ablation explains the gap: affinity raises KV hit rate, and LPT placement reduces imbalance from 3.46×3.46\times to 1.24×1.24\times, moving the measured SLO knee from 240 to at least 500 QPS.




We make three contributions:


• 



a prefix-affinity router that plans cache locality and expected load together;


• 



a six-policy hardware evaluation centered on a 70B model and 60 H100 GPUs, with paired runs, a second workload distribution, and burst experiments; and


• 



a measured operating envelope that includes loss and tie regimes, plus evidence for using shadow replay instead of an analytic residency predictor.






Top-rate admission and LPT are established techniques; we do not claim a new scheduling primitive. The contribution lies in the routing design, its large-scale measurements, and the conditions under which operators should leave the ordinary load balancer in place.
